red_flags: Rigid, silent abdomen with the patient lying still — perforation with peritonitis; urgent surgical referral
Hypotension, syncope, or back pain with a pulsatile abdominal mass — ruptured aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise; urgent surgical referral
Severe pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen in an elderly patient or one with atrial fibrillation — mesenteric ischemia; urgent surgical referral
Feculent vomiting with distension and absolute constipation — established intestinal obstruction
Acute abdomen with a missed period or positive pregnancy test in a woman of childbearing age — ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise
Cold, sweaty, tachycardic patient whatever the presumed cause — shock in an acute abdomen
exam: Record BP, pulse, temperature, and respiratory rate — look for shock and fever
Inspect the abdomen for distension, visible peristalsis, and surgical scars
Palpate all quadrants for guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness — start away from the pain
Palpate deliberately for an expansile pulsatile mass above the umbilicus
Percuss for loss of liver dullness (free air) and for tympanitic distension
Auscultate bowel sounds — absent (peritonitis/ileus) vs high-pitched tinkling (obstruction)
Examine both hernial orifices in every patient — an obstructed femoral hernia is easily missed
Elicit Murphy's sign at the right costal margin
Test McBurney's point tenderness and Rovsing's sign
Feel femoral pulses on both sides — asymmetry with a tender abdomen points to aortic pathology
Perform a rectal examination — tenderness, mass, melena, or empty ballooned rectum

investigations.why: Leukocytosis supports appendicitis, cholecystitis, or perforation; a falling hemoglobin supports ruptured aneurysm or ectopic pregnancy over the non-bleeding differentials
Markedly raised rules in acute pancreatitis; mild elevation can occur with perforated ulcer or mesenteric ischemia, so interpret against the exam

investigations.test: Erect chest X-ray + supine abdominal X-ray
investigations.why: Free air under the diaphragm rules in perforation; dilated loops with air-fluid levels rule in obstruction — separates the two operative emergencies from colic
Hematuria supports ureteric colic; pyuria and nitrites point away from the surgical differentials toward urinary infection

investigations.test: Urine pregnancy test (all women of childbearing age)
investigations.why: A positive test with an acute abdomen makes ectopic pregnancy the working diagnosis and changes the whole pathway
Assesses dehydration from vomiting in obstruction and pancreatitis; unexplained acidosis-range picture with lactate supports mesenteric ischemia
Inferior myocardial infarction mimics epigastric pain; atrial fibrillation on the trace raises mesenteric embolism among the differentials
First-line: free fluid (perforation, rupture, ectopic), gallstones with a thick-walled gallbladder (cholecystitis), aortic diameter (aneurysm), and hydronephrosis (ureteric colic)
Second-line — if the diagnosis is still unclear after X-ray and ultrasound: defines obstruction level and cause, confirms mesenteric ischemia, and finds contained aneurysm leak
